speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: Hello, everyone. Welcome to a new episode of The Dissenter. I'm your host, as always, Ricardo Lops, and today I'm joined by Doctors James Tilley and Sarah Hoboldt. Uh, Doctor Tilley is professor of politics in the Department of Politics and International relations at the University of Oxford and Dr. Hoboldt holds the Sutherland Chair in the European Institutions and is also the head of the department of government at the London School of Economics and Political Science. And today we're going to talk about their book Tribal Politics How Brexit Divided Britain. So Dr. Tilley, Dr. Hoboldt, welcome to the show. It's a huge pleasure to everyone.

speaker: James Tilley
words: Thanks very much for inviting me.

speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: OK, so, uh, before we get into the sort of political science that you explore in your book related to Brexit and the political tribal tribalism that derived from it, uh, tell us first. A little bit about the history of Brexit. So what led to it, uh, to it, I mean, in the history of, uh, the politics of the United Kingdom, what preceded Brexit?

speaker: Sara Hobolt
words: I mean, I think the first thing to say here is that Brexit was by no means inevitable. Sometimes when we look back now that Brexit has happened, we might think, oh, you know, all roads would lead to this outcome. There was this sort of major desire or public interest in having A referendum on membership, but that was really far from the case. In fact, when we, which we do in the book, we trace public opinion on European membership, the first thing to note is really that people didn't care very much about the EU or EU membership. So when David Cameron, uh, the Prime Minister who called the referendum, when he first promised the referendum back in 2013, only about 2% of the British population even mentioned it as one of the most salient issues. And in the, in the election that came after that in 2015, it wasn't really one of the debated issues at all. It was not even in the top 10 of issues that people cared most about. So it wasn't the sort of public salience that led to the referendum. But the issue of EU membership had been an issue of conflict and debate in British politics for a long time, but mainly amongst political elites. So first, the Labour Party and then the Conservative Party were really divided on the issue of EU membership, and that was the primary reason why David Cameron decided to hold the referendum, because he wanted to quell or appease the. Divisions within his own party and there was also new pressures from the Eurosceptic UKIP party on the right and so he thought by having that referendum he could sort of solve that issue within his party in that way because of course he expected to win the referendum. So by winning that issue it would sort of put a line on there and say now we've dealt with Europe, so. So that's really what was so interesting and what we deal with in our book Tribal Policy is that EU membership went from an issue that most people didn't care that much about. It wasn't particularly salient to an issue that came to be a political identity, something that really defined how people looked at themselves and how they looked at the world.

speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: But historically, were there any precedents to Brexit in Britain or or was it something unprecedented and if it was unprecedented, in what ways was it unprecedented?

speaker: Sara Hobolt
words: So it's not unprecedented in Britain or indeed elsewhere in Europe. We've had, you know, over 50 referendums on aspects of European integration and particularly there's a very clear historical precedent in Britain which is 1975. So in 1975 there was a similar referendum. So Britain had joined the European Union, uh, together with Ireland and Denmark in 1973, um, but the Labour Party at the time had was split on it. And so we had a Labour Prime Minister in 1975, Harold Wilson, who decided again. In a similar parallel to what happened with David Cameron in 2016, his own party was divided on the issue, so perhaps the referendum would be seen as a good way of solving that issue. So again, we have these internal party tensions this time within the Labour Party that led to a referendum on in-out membership at that time of the European Economic Community. So that's a very clear parallel. Now that's sort of where the similarities stopped because of course what happened in 1975 was a very big victory for staying in the EEC. So about 2 to 1 of people voted to stay in the EEC. So that meant not that the issue in a sense went away, particularly within the parties. It sort of rumbled on, but it meant that because it was a vote in favor of state. QUO. It didn't become this sort of shock where there was continuous negotiations about how the new arrangements should look like. Instead it was like, OK, people have now voted quite emphatically to stay in the EEC. We can now continue that way. So it continued as an elite sort of issue of conflict, but not as a sort of big public salient issue.

speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: So talking about the referendum itself, because I mean I might be misremembering a little bit because back in 2016 I didn't really follow it extremely closely, but I remember that when the results came out, people, many people. WERE sort of surprised that Brexit had won, that leaving the European Union had won. So, but were there any signs that that could happen before it did, or and what was its immediate fallout?

speaker: James Tilley
words: Um, I mean, I think actually the interesting thing there is that. While perhaps there were some perceptions that it was a done deal for Remain that Remain would win, actually the polls were very, very close for the whole 6 months beforehand. I mean, you're talking about like maybe a 1% lead on average, which was pretty much unchanging, um, over that period. And I think that's really important for our story because it meant there were two evenly sized groups in the population basically pitted against each other. And I think the other important thing for our story is sort of the the opposite of what happened in 1975. Um, THAT it was, uh, not only close, but it was also a vote for change. So 75, it's, it's a big majority for staying in the EU and it's also the status quo. 2016, very, very tight result and a vote against the status quo. And so I think the immediate fallout, which is actually really relevant, um, uh, for, for what we're interested in, is that everyone therefore had to decide what Brexit actually meant. And how it was going to be enacted and all of that was going to take some period of time during which this would be a very, very salient issue, unlike as Sara was saying beforehand when basically no one really, um, cared about it. So these two things are really crucial to our stories, these evenly sized groups, a tight results, and a big constitutional question that then needs to be decided over a period of time, um, after the actual referendum.

speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: Mhm. But in the immediate aftermath, I mean, how did the people across the country react to it, across the United Kingdom? I mean, were people mostly surprised? Were people sort of expecting that result, or what?

speaker: James Tilley
words: Um, I think the. I would say there was a degree of surprise because of the way in which the, the polling had been interpreted to indicate that because Remain had a lead most of the time, that meant they were going to win. um, AND so I think there was a degree of surprise because of that, and I think there was also a degree of surprise amongst elites, and that's most elites. So if you think about what I mean by that, let's say academics, journalists, um, most politicians were on the side of Remain. And as we're going to talk about, people like to project what they think, uh, how the world is, uh, how the world, uh, should be and pretend that that's how the world is. And so I think a lot of them were surprised because they didn't, they themselves perhaps didn't meet many people who were going to vote leave and so didn't, and, and therefore didn't really quite believe that it was close. Um, AND so I think surprise was more concentrated amongst those people than perhaps it was among the general public in some ways.

speaker: Sara Hobolt
words: And famously, of course, apparently the, the, the leaders of the leave camp themselves, including Boris Johnson, was quite surprised and sort of slept through it. At least that's the, uh, that's the sort of modern political history of the event that he had to, that he wasn't awake. And then he had to go and give this speech because one of the things that, and, and we write about in the that that is quite telling that it wasn't only this event, which I think you're right, was to many people, particularly that the opinion formers was surprising, but it was also the fact that there wasn't really a clear plan, a roadmap. Had we voted by the same margin, 52 to 48 to stay in, it was pretty clear, you know, not much would have happened. But all of a sudden there was this result where There wasn't a clear roadmap, not by the official leave campaign, you know, in fact, many people had campaigned for slightly different things, of course. Then you have a Prime Minister, David Cameron resigning, and so you have to then have, and so, so there were a lot of things that were not settled, so it wasn't just the immediate surprise, but also the fact all of a sudden people We, oh my goodness, what do we do now, including probably some quite central figures in the on the leave side that there wasn't a kind of a, they never had to have had a clear agreement or roadmap for what that leave, what Brexit would would look like and of course we all know that Theresa May kept saying Brexit means Brexit, and everyone was like, well, that's a sort of slight tautology, and that was partly to avoid this discussion of what that actually meant while they were figuring it out within the party.

speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: Right, so we're going to talk more about Brexit and its consequences, but I would like to now do it by exploring the central topics that you talk about in your book. So since we're going to talk about political tribalism here, what is actually a tribal politics? I mean, what is tribalism in the, in the political context?

speaker: James Tilley
words: I mean that's a, that is a good question. It is obviously at the heart of the book. The book's called Tribal Politics after all. Um, I think, uh, there's a number of different aspects we could talk about, but I, I think there's two kind of key elements that we sort of focus on in the book and I think probably we're going to focus on in our discussion too. And the first is about, uh, in-groups versus out-groups, us versus them. So the idea that we create, um, we adopt, we join a political group that we consider to be ours, um, in some way. We feel attached to people in that group, we feel attached to the identity, attached to the label, um, and part of that is also, therefore, uh, disliking people in the out-group. Having prejudice against, against people in the out-group and in favor of the in-group, discriminating against the out-group, discriminating in favor of the, uh, the in-group, um, and I think that's the first, Element, um, of what we think of as political tribalism. I think the second element is sort of, uh, sometimes easy to overlook, but it's actually perhaps in, in some ways more important, and that's the way we kind of construct the world around us based on those group identities or we construct our perceptions of the world around us. So we sort of see reality through the lens of the political, um, identity. Adopt policy positions on the basis of it. We might judge how well or badly democracy is functioning through that lens, uh, and so on. So it's these kind of two things. On the first hand, uh, on the one hand, you've got this kind of in-group out-group dynamics, and then you've also, on the other hand, got this kind of consequences of those in-group out-group dynamics in terms of how it shapes, uh, the way we see and interact with, in our case, the political world, but also I guess more broadly the social world. We might perhaps talk a bit about both of those, um, later on.

speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: Yeah, right, so the two political tribes that developed after Brexit or during Brexit and then more so after it, you call them in your book the leavers and the Remainers. How did each of them develop and what would you say characterizes them and makes them opposites of one another?

speaker: James Tilley
words: So I think the first thing to say there is that it's not just that we call them leavers and remainers, it's that they call themselves levers and remainers. And so these aren't, these aren't labels we are attaching to groups. They're the labels the groups themselves use to describe both their own group and the other group. And that's actually a really important part of what's, of, of, of what we're interested in, um, so. The vast majority of people who voted in the referendum subsequently identified themselves as Leavers and Remainers, about 80% of people, um, immediately after the referendum, and in fact, today, so 10 years after the referendum, 60% of people still are willing to call themselves a Leaver or Remainer. They still think of themselves in that way, um, which is about the same amount of people, maybe even slightly more, more than the number of people who are willing to identify as a political party supporter. So just to give you sort of context for that. Um How did they develop? Well, I think, um. I mean, they developed ultimately and sort of Sarah touched on this right at the beginning because of the people being forced to make a choice at the referendum, so to vote for one side or the other, you had to convert your position on an issue, an issue which most people didn't really have a very strong view on, but they had maybe some vague view on, uh, EU integration, and then convert that view into picking one side or the other, and then you became part of one group or the other. Um, IN fact, I mean, the, the names Leavers and Remainers, I mean, the, the, that, they, they're derived from the options on the ballot paper. You could vote to leave or vote to remain. So you could have had a yes, no, you know, option, and then people perhaps would have been yeses and, um, and, uh, and noers or nayers, as they're sometimes called in Scotland, where it was a yes, no kind of outcome for the Scottish independence referendum. Um, SO I think the really crucial thing to understand is that. What characterizes these two groups is how they voted in the referendum, yeah, it's the issue position, uh, that they held, but then the choice that they made in June 2016 for one option, um, or the other. I mean, we, we might want to talk a bit about the social characteristics of both sides as well, perhaps if you want, but I think the. The essence of having an issue-based identity, which is what we think this is, is you have a position at issue, you then are forced to make a choice, a binary choice in this case, and then that creates two groups, which are going to be naturally, um, in opposition, uh, to one another. Um, I think the only thing perhaps to add to that is, is also worth just saying, the nature of an issue position on any political issue is lots of people are in the middle. Um, AND that's true for the EU, uh, issue as well. But those people, they went into the referendum and they had to make a choice. So they might, so two people might have had quite similar views actually on EU integration, but when they went and voted, one voted to leave and one voted remain. And so subsequently, they became leavers and remainers. So the the translation of the issue position into the, um, identity means that you've got a spectrum. That then becomes a sort of binary set of categories, um, that's what we call two categories. So it's, it's kind of a different, uh, a different kind of idea. It's a, quite an important element of how these issues become identities effectively. I think.

speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: Yeah, but this sort of tribalistic dynamics that can develop in the political realm, let's say. I mean, can something like this happen around any sort of potential uh topic or issue, or is it that, er, when it comes to Brexit, it had certain types of characteristics that made it, er, that people who fell on either the leaver or remainer camp. Uh, BECAME that for, uh, that tribalistic.

speaker: Sara Hobolt
words: I mean, I think, I think the starting point in terms of how we look at it is that it isn't really about the nature of the issue or even how strongly people feel about the issue to start off with, because as we talked about, in fact, people didn't feel particularly strongly about the EU or it wasn't something that affected their lives very much. Of course you're always going to get a hardcore people who are Europhiles or really Eurosceptics, but they were a tiny minority in Britain. Um, IN fact, most people were sort of maybe broadly we call kind of indifferent Eurosceptics, uh, in the book. So they were sort of a bit skeptical, uh, uh, of the whole European thing, but that didn't necessarily mean that they had to, um, You know, you know, they would vote to leave. I mean, exactly what happened with the referendum is it created these two, it compelled people to be in one or two camps. So the starting point is people have, there are lots of political issues. Most of them don't become identities, but some do, and that's really part of a social and political process, and, and, and what. Brexit was this sort of Goldilocks combination of factors that created the conditions where an issue like Europe did become something that became really at the heart of it became a tribal issue with two camps, so it's not just about, oh, it couldn't happen to other issues, but it's also not, oh it happens to most political issues,

speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: right, I understand. And how is the discussion surrounding Brexit Brexit evolved over these past 10 years? I mean, are people really still that entrenched when it comes to their tribalism surrounding this topic, if of course they fall on the camp of the leavers or the Remainers and not in the middle, or are people. More, uh, tribalized or more polarized when it comes to that issue nowadays than they were 10 years ago in the immediate aftermath of the referendum or how have things evolved basically?

speaker: Sara Hobolt
words: I think uh we can sort of look at two things here. One is the issue about how the identities have evolved, and another is sort of what are are general attitudes also amongst those who don't hold identities on Brexit. And when it comes to the identities, I think what's really quite extraordinary is how sticky they've been. We're now more than a decade on from the referendum. If you read British newspapers or watch British television or listen to, you know, even our new Prime Minister, you won't hear Andy Burnham talk a lot about Brexit. Uh, IN fact, uh, the Labour Party, I think, quite deliberately avoids talking a lot about it. So it's not really as a sort of headline news the way it was for, you know, 56 years, constantly bombarded with news about Brexit. Everything was about Brexit. So if you just look at the news coverage, you would think, oh, Brexit is over, it's done. But if you look at, uh, and we've traced really across a decade public opinion and identities, you see that because it's more than your opinion. It is these identities about how we see ourselves, they have that stickiness to it. So as James mentioned, we still have over 60% of people still identifying as either leave or remainer. Even the term remainer doesn't really make sense anymore because we've, of course, left the EU, but it's still something people use to describe themselves. So that's quite extraordinary in that way and also really shows that how it's more than just an issue of opinion. Now that's even higher amongst those people who voted back in 2016. Now, so if we look on the other hand, at attitudes towards Brexit, it might look like there's been a shift, and so how do we reconcile that? So if we look at now, we ask people, do you think it was a good thing or a bad thing for the United Kingdom to leave the European Union, there's now quite a big majority that would say that it's a bad thing, yeah. Uh, SORT of, um, in the region of kind of, uh, uh, 55, 60% who consistently, it would say it's a bad thing. Um, NOW, that has to do with not so much that lots of people who identify strongly as leaders have changed their minds. That's not really what's going on. Of course, there will be some people who've changed their minds, but a couple of things are going on. One is just demographic change. So if you look at how The population in Britain has evolved for the last decade. Older people were more likely to be leavers than younger people, and they're the ones who have sadly, some of them left the electorate, while the younger people who can now vote are more likely to say, to be more positive about the EU. And another thing is for those people who didn't vote back in 2016 or who didn't develop an identity, they're more likely to say, oh, this sounds like this Brexit thing was a bad thing. So we have seen a kind of shift. Even if we ask about the question of rejoin, uh, it's now about 55% who would rejoin. Uh, THAT you, uh, if, if you ask it in that way, um, uh, so, so there has been a sort of more EU positive or Brexit negative shift, but the, the main thing in terms of, uh, the identities is that they're still there in quite high numbers, uh, despite the sort of the lower salience of the issue.

speaker: James Tilley
words: And I think one thing to add to that is that there's, there's very few people sort of hint that there's very few people switching between the identities. They've become quite fixed with those people. Maybe some people have left the identity, they've gone to not having one at all, but they've not switched sides. And so most of the, most of the kind of change in sort of those headline numbers that, um, Sarah mentioned about support for say, rejoining, that's actually coming from people who didn't develop an identity, um, in, in 2016 or in the immediate aftermath.

speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: Right, uh, yes, I, I'm going to ask you more about issue-based identities in a second, but just before that, when it comes to social identities, is it that people identifying as leavers or remainers track onto any sort of demographics, like, for example, I remember that. Right after Brexit, there were people trying to make sense of what might have caused people to vote one way or the other, and they were talking, for example, that it was really about the young versus the older people with high educational attainment versus low educational attainment and They also, certain people also tried to make it about uh class divisions. I mean that people who were low socioeconomic status were more likely to be leavers and uh high socioeconomic status, more like. TO be remainder, things like that. I mean, is any of that true? And if so, do any of those sort of social categories track onto this division or not?

speaker: James Tilley
words: Um, I think that's that's yes and no. Um, SO I'll start with the yes and then I'll go on the no perhaps. Um, I think the, the yes is that like with most political attitudes, there are social characteristics, exactly the ones you mentioned in this case, um, age, education, to some extent, social class. In our case, actually national identity, um, would be the one that do predict people's views about the European, um, Union. Education is probably the best of those things that you mentioned in terms of the predictor. And they also predicted, therefore, how people voted in the, um, referendum. Um, THAT'S the yes bit. I think the no bit though is that. They're not very good predictors of people's attitudes and people's vote, and I think that that's quite surprising, I think, to some people because exactly like you just said, the referendum is sometimes presented as a, you know, a class conflict or an age conflict or or whatever it is, um, but I think some of that's really about people. You know, humans like to be able to sort of describe the person on either side in this case, and so we sort of reach for these things that might be, you know, relatively slightly correlated with the, with these issue opinions, and then we describe or think of people in those, in those ways, but Actually, if we model people's vote choice at the referendum, you know, using these kind of social characteristics and, you know, at least the models we use, we've got a very long list, they're very well measured, um, and some really good measures of national identity, but we don't actually do a very good job of predicting, um, how someone voted. And there's, there's sort of 22 reasons for that. One is that the, simply the relationship between those characteristics and people's vote is just not that strong, um. But the second bit, which is perhaps a bit more subtle, is that where there is strength, the strength is at the extremes. So by that, what I mean is, let's say we took education. So people with very high levels of education, um, so people with a PhD, say, um. They tend to be, uh, much more supportive of EU membership than the average person, but there's not very many people with a PhD out there. So you could sort of say, well, education is a good predictor, but it's only a good predictor for a small segment of the population at the extremes, and then the same is true for, say, national identity. So people who thought of themselves as Europeans, having a European nationality were much more likely to be supportive of EU membership, but prior to the referendum, um, we might get onto it perhaps later on after the referendum because it's changed a bit, prior to the referendum, very few people thought of themselves as European, yeah, something about 10, 15% of the population. So the kind of characteristics we have don't really do a very good job of, um, uh, of actually explaining how people, uh, how people voted. So the amount of variation we can explain in people's opinions is actually not, um, not terribly high. So, you know, it's not that leavers are just a, a, another name for the working class and Remainers are just another name, um, for the middle class. They're kind of new political identities. Um, RATHER than just, um, sort of old ones, uh, with a different label, uh, attached to them.

speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: So I would like to hear more from you about issue-based identity. So what causes issue-based identities? I mean what leads to the development or what are the factors that Help to convert an issue into an identity and in the book you explore things like issue contestation, issue expression, and issue alignment. So could you tell us about that?

speaker: Sara Hobolt
words: Perhaps, uh, a good place to start is what is what a social identity is because what we're interested here is really issue-based identity as a type of social identity, and that's really what makes it different from having an opinion on a political issue. So, you know, social identity is a sense of who we are as people based on what group we belong to. And we have lots of these social identities. So, you know, I might have a social identity as a, you know, an academic and a political scientist and a Londoner and a Danish person, and they sort of form my perception of who I am, but also who I'm not, like who are the people who are not like that. So, Both gives me a kind of a sense of, of worth and self-esteem, uh, in terms of basis of I, I belong to these groups, but it can also sometimes, if these identities are polarized, it can also then be a source of, you know, outgroup prejudice and discrimination against the people who are not like that. Like sometimes, uh, uh, I think about it, uh, you know, yesterday I went to a football match. I always think this is like the pinnacle of where you can really see, you know, these social identities and outgroup things in action, because here you have, you know, I just happen to have Fulham ticket, you know, Fulham season tickets, which is sort of a bit random in a way. But once you're sitting there in the stands, you're like, we're the best, and these other guys are complete losers and sort of worse words. So that's the sort of the in-group feeling. Uh, AND also the outgroup animus in, in play. Now, so, so that's a social identity and often, uh, the literature and political science have focused a lot on social identities that were based on more, we might think of as scriptive characteristics like, oh, it might be race, or it might be Gender, it might be class or, or, or partisanship, which is the perhaps the most powerful social political based social identity that we often think of that predicts all sorts of things like attitudes and voting behavior and so on. And so the, to, to answer your question, to get to issue-based identity, that's really where you have a political issue that where you form an that you have a view on, and you form an identity on the basis of other people holding the same view on that issue. Uh, AND, and, and some people holding the opposite view or a different view. Now, of course, we have lots of views on, on things in, in politics and policy that never, you know, lead to an identity. I might like low taxes or I might like regular bin collection, but I don't go around thinking, oh, I'm the sort of once a week bin collector person or the low tax, even the low tax person. I mean, some people might have an identity based on that, but most don't. It's just views you have, yeah. So, so really what we, you know, that's why it's the sort of the puzzle, one of the puzzles of the book is, so when does, as we show quite clearly, an issue become um uh something that's the basis of an identity and also the basis of tribal politics. And, and as I mentioned before, that's really a part of not just really the issue itself, but the how that issue plays out politically and socially. And that's why we have these, these 3, kind of, you know, conditions to sort of think about how could that work beyond Brexit, the sort of issue contestation, uh, issue expression, and also lack of issue alignment. Uh, HAPPY to, to sort of elaborate on that, but that's, that's really, that's really where we get from the social identity, the issue identity.

speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: Yes, please elaborate a little bit more on that, particularly on the factor related to issue alignment.

speaker: Sara Hobolt
words: Yes, so, so, um, so the three factors are really ones where we all see them in Brexit, but we also think that they could characterize why other issues become identities. So starting with. CONTESTATION, not surprisingly for an issue to become an identity, something people feel strongly and emotively about. It has to be something that's heavily contested, sort of very salient, not only salient, but also where there's considerable disagreement between, you know, political actors, between people in the population. So in Brexit, of course, we went from a point where this was not a heavily contested issue, but by calling a referendum, all of a sudden, it became everything everyone talked about, and that didn't stop with the referendum. We then had 56 years where it was all everyone talked about, because it was then the question of what Brexit, what does it look like? And a constant refighting of this issue. Should we really remain in the EU? Would there be a no-deal Brexit, and so on. So it was constantly contested. Now, the second thing is what we call issue expression, because sometimes issues can be contested at the elite level, but we as citizens never really have to commit. And that's with a lot of issues like the taxation issue. Oh, we might have views, but we're not really committing. We might be in the sort of middle, oh, I like low taxes, but I also like a big welfare state, but I'm never really asked to commit, am I in the low tax, small state, or in the high tax, high state category. I just sort of can have my cake and eat it. Now what happened when there's issue expression is you have to commit in some way, uh, uh, on one side or the other. Now, of course, what we do in an election or in a referendum, here you had all these people, many of whom were in the middle, they committed, they were compelled to either vote. Physically go down, put a cross. Now, once I've put that cross, I can no longer be this, you know, ambivalent person in the middle, because I have committed to saying no, in fact, I am a leaver, and I then have to sort of keep thinking about, well, I'd like to, I don't like to be wrong. So once I've said, OK, leave is the way it goes, then when news comes out, oh, maybe Brexit wasn't good, I'm like, Oh, that's not great, because I can't be wrong, because I took the right choice. I committed to that choice. So I will see things through that lens. Similarly, if I vote to remain, I'm going to interpret everything like, God, Brexit was terrible, and I was right all along. So that's the sort of issue expression. Now, that's not just a vote, we can, you know, some people, I'm sure you know, people like that, they go on social media. And they express, they recommit to their issue, you know, to their view on a particular issue, or in the case of Brexit, we had the biggest online petition ever of people who said they wanted a second referendum or people's vote on the EU.
